newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 11.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--A coordinating mechanism that will provide detailed briefings and information companies attempting to gain a toehold in the Balkans and southeast Europe is one of the factors that would held Greek businesses penetrate these regions, according to those attending a meeting organised by the Federation of Greek Industries (SEV), Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos and Development Minister Vasso Papandreou. SEV officials said the major problems affecting companies working in the region fell into three types - the institutional, operational and political.

--A 1928 legal provisions governing the operation of the Athens Stock Exchange will be used in a complex procedure to pull Katsoulis Securities - faced with failing to meet clients' commitments last week - out of trouble.
--Interest rates on five-, seven- and ten-year state titles will remain stable for the July 17 auction, according to the finance ministry. Interest rates will range between 9.2-8.9 percent.

--The government's next economic meeting - most probably next Tuesday - will be forced to decide on structural measures to bolster the 1997 state budget following the news that public revenues increased in the first half-year by only 11-12 percent, which, if it continues, will mean a 500 billion drachma shortfall in budget targets at the end of the year.

--Companies will face a tax bill of between 13-15 billion drachmas this year for their real estate holdings. Sources say that the figure was calculated on the basis of latest results from the four major tax bureaux in the country.

--The National Bank of Greece is now turning enthusiastically to the possibility of providing financing for public orgnisations and enterprises (DEKOs). Reports say that National has already completed planning of a programme to conquer this market, involving both drachma and foreign exchange lending.

--There were objections to the government and transport ministry's choice of managing consultant of Hellenic Railways when the decision came to the relevant committee for approval. The candidate's laconic responses to committee members' questions raised tempers and eyebrow. Reports state that the government will withdraw the candidacy.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis will chair a meeting next week to examine the course of the budget and inflation and possible measures that could be adopted and recommended in the recently-released Spraos report. Bank of Greece Governor Lucas Papademos will also attend the meeting, according to reports.

--Greeks are the worst in paying off their debts, according to a new study by the Commission. The study found that Greeks took an average of 94 days to pay off credit bills, compared to a contractural limit of 75 days plus nine for delays.

--Despite a nominal improvement in the current account deficit in March, the picture presented for the first quarter is not good. The cumulative current account deficit was up 35.2 percent to $1.627 billion in the first quarter compared to the same period last year.
